Q: How can I sparsely check out only one single file from a Git repository? A:

I don’t see what worked for me listed out here, so I will include it should anybody be in my situation.

My situation, I have a remote repository of maybe 10,000 files and I need to build an RPM file for my Linux system. The build of the RPM includes a Git clone of everything. All I need is one file to start the RPM build. I can clone the entire source tree which does what I need, but it takes an extra two minutes to download all those files when all I need is one. I tried to use the Git archive option discussed, and I got “fatal: Operation not supported by protocol.”

It seems I have to get some sort of archive option enabled on the server, and my server is maintained by bureaucratic thugs that seem to enjoy making it difficult to get things done.

What I finally did was I went into the web interface for Bitbucket and viewed the one file I needed. I did a right click on the link to download a raw copy of the file and selected “copy shortcut” from the resulting popup. I could not just download the raw file because I needed to automate things and I don’t have a browser interface on my Linux server.

For the sake of discussion, that resulted in the URL:

https://ourArchive.ourCompany.com/projects/ThisProject/repos/data/raw/foo/bar.spec?at=refs%2Fheads%2FTheBranchOfInterest

I could not directly download this file from the Bitbucket repository, because I needed to sign in first. After a little digging, I found this worked: On Linux:

echo "myUser:myPass123"| base64
bXlVc2VyOm15UGFzczEyMwo=

curl -H 'Authorization: Basic bXlVc2VyOm15UGFzczEyMwo=' 'https://ourArchive.ourCompany.com/projects/ThisProject/repos/data/raw/foo/bar.spec?at=refs%2Fheads%2FTheBranchOfInterest' > bar.spec

This combination allowed me to download the one file I needed to build everything else.

Q: What does "local variable" mean in the Forth programming language? A:

In Forth, local variables are described by the following syntax (see also 13.6.2.2550 {:):

{: args [ | vals ] [ –– outs ] :}

where each of args, vals and outs represents space-delimited names (the parts in square brackets are optional). These names are interpreted as follows:

  • args names are for locals that are initialized from the data stack, with the top of the stack being assigned to the rightmost name in args;
  • vals names are for locals that are uninitialized;
  • outs names are ignored (they are for documentation purposes only, if any).

Gforth uses { ... } notation for locals as an alternative to the standard one.

So, swap can be defined as:

: swap {: a b :} b a ;

It takes two values from the stack into a and b local variables, and then puts them back on the stack in the reversed order.

An example of use an uninitialized local variable:

: exch ( x2 addr -- x1 ) {: a | x1 :}
  a @ to x1 a ! x1
;

The optional -- ... part is allowed to mimic a stack diagram, i.e., to unite the declaration of locals and the stack diagram for a word. For example:

: umin {: u2 u1 -- u2|u1 :} u2 u1 u< if u2 else u1 then ;

Without special optimizations, performance of local variables is slightly worse than of a little stack juggling.

Update: See also archived thread from comp.lang.forth, 2024 (mentioned in my comment below). Local variables are reported to reduce performance by 9%-17% in Gforth.

Q: Why doesn't RestrictedPython allow iter, max, min, sum, etc A:

They want to be able to perform access checks when user code tries to retrieve an item from a sequence or other iterable. RestrictedPython can compile seq[0] to code that performs an access check, but it can't do that cleanly with min, max, or sum.

The default min, max, and sum all allow retrieving sequence items without performing access checks. For example,

container = # some one-element list

x = min(container)
y = max(container)

class Foo:
    def __add__(self, other):
        return other

z = sum(container, start=Foo())

RestrictedPython is a Zope project, and you can see in Zope's closely-related AccessControl framework how they define guarded wrappers for min, max, and sum and use those in place of the built-ins.

iter is similar. They want to perform access checks on every item retrieved from the iterator, so AccessControl defines a SafeIter wrapper that performs access checks and a guarded_iter function that wraps any iterator in a SafeIter if it's not already known to be safe. This function is installed in place of the default iter. (It's also the same function that provides the access checks for guarded_min, guarded_max, and guarded_sum.)

Q: How do I prevent redaction rectangles from removing surrounding text? A:

The redaction rectangles in general can be as small as you like as long as they are not empty. So you could take the rect returned form search and create a rectangle of height 1 around the horizontal middle line. This is large enough for applying the redaction and (hopefully!) small enough to avoid anything else intruding into it.

h2 = rect.height / 2 - 0.5  # half the height, reduced somewhat
red_rect = rect + (0, h2, 0, -h2)  # leaves a small horizontal stripe of height 1

The only concern: If any images need to be redacted as well, then holes are punched into them that definitely are too small!

Another approach: Use the text extraction option pymupdf.TEXT_ACCURATE_BBOXES. This creates tight bboxes around the text - leaving no space above or below. Better than the other suggestion using small glyph heights. It also is independent from any (potentially broken) font properties, because it only looks at the Bézier curves that create a glyph.

Q: How to convert JSON to tabular data using Power Automate? A:

Without seeing the configuration of the Power BI table visualization in question, the Total row is likely "cosmetic" in a certain sense – in that Power BI is conveniently calculating and displaying that summary per the visual's specific configuration on top of the underlying data. The DAX query is returning just the unsummarized data. It's up to you to figure out how you want to summarize it wherever you're moving it to.

Unfortunately, the Power Automate conenctor for Excel lacks functionality to configure summary rows the same way you could in the typical Excel UI. A janky solution would be to Create the table, then Add a row to that table and fill it with your own incremental calculations of the total figure(s) you're looking to get.

Q: Why does `printf ... if ( $verbose)` result in a taint error A:

It's due to a documented limitation of the taint system.

As explained in perlsec (where the taint mechanism is documented),

For efficiency reasons, Perl takes a conservative view of whether data is tainted. If an expression contains tainted data, any subexpression may be considered tainted, even if the value of the subexpression is not itself affected by the tainted data.

A more detailed explanation follows, and solutions follow that.

The taint system attempts to prevent the execution of user-provided code. The taint system considers the template passed to printf to be code. As such, passing a tainted value as printf's first operand results in a taint error.

$ perl -T -e'printf "$ARGV[0]\n"' 1
Insecure dependency in printf while running with -T switch at -e line 1.

Even though the following could be considered to suffer from a injection bug, it doesn't rely on user-provided input, so it doesn't result in a taint error.

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; printf "$me\n"'
foo

Also, flow control based on user-provided input doesn't result in execution of the user-provided input, so it doesn't result in a taint error either.

$ perl -T -e'print "foo\n" if $ARGV[0]' 1
foo

So why does combining the two result in a taint error?

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; printf "$me\n" if $ARGV[0]' 1
Insecure dependency in printf while running with -T switch at -e line 1.

To answer that, we must be aware that EXPR2 if EXPR1; and EXPR1 and EXPR2; compile to the same code internally. This means the preceding is identical to the following:

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; $ARGV[0] and printf "$me\n"' 1
Insecure dependency in printf while running with -T switch at -e line 1.

And that behaviour is explained in perlsec, where the taint mechanism is documented.

For efficiency reasons, Perl takes a conservative view of whether data is tainted. If an expression contains tainted data, any subexpression may be considered tainted, even if the value of the subexpression is not itself affected by the tainted data.

The best way to address this is to stop interpolating into the template. Such code injections invite problems.

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; printf "%s\n", $me if $ARGV[0]' 1
foo

But you could also ensure that the printf is its own statement.

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; do { printf "$me\n" } if $ARGV[0]' 1
foo

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; if ( $ARGV[0] ) { printf "$me\n" }' 1
foo
